name: Tomas Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas, 58, an experienced mid-level electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at the ordinary wiring and repairs we do in homes and small businesses, not a crew leader or a specialist somebody calls across the country. Yesterday I replaced damaged light fittings and wrote down the test results before the shop opened. I use AI occasionally for a checked explanation after a colleague has shown me a proven method, and I still prefer being shown a new instrument before trusting my first reading.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mina translates appliance instruction leaflets, our grown children live elsewhere, and we own our small flat outright. My firm pays more than the usual rate, we have fourteen months of expenses saved, and plenty of electrical employers are nearby, though no other job is promised. My own wage covers ordinary essentials, with Mina's fees providing more household room, so current living feels secure. I'd like to understand when stopping work could be affordable, but retirement income, a date and our actual later needs haven't been confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a checked explanation can be useful without replacing the electrician who takes the reading. I'd let the people using a tool show what it improved. I'd rather compare the actual result than argue about whether everybody had been fooled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current work and living would feel secure, with my higher wage covering essentials and fourteen months saved. Mina's ordinary translation work carries on in this picture, and we have the flat we already own. I'd still want actual later income figures, but not knowing my stopping date isn't the same as missing the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current paid electrical repairs now and through the next year, with normal tests and the occasional checked AI explanation I already use. I'd ask our grown daughter for time sorting old employment letters only if she was willing and available, counting no money from her. We'd mark missing information as missing rather than turn the old letters into a retirement income estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our actual living, and pleased to have time for a small useful household task. I'd still be irritated by a folder with three copies of one letter and none of the next. A tidy folder would please me without proving when I could retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask your daughter if you feel financially secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because she might be willing to spend an hour sorting with us, not because she's responsible for paying the bills. I'd ask about her actual time before making an afternoon of it. If she couldn't, the papers would remain our job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new AI service to read the letters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd first sort what we actually had and ask the actual provider about missing entries. A smooth explanation of an old letter wouldn't confirm a payment. I wouldn't treat ordinary checked tool use at work as new learning just because you asked about AI.

say: I'd judge **checked explanations** by the actual result rather than whether a technology prediction sounded impressive.
I'd let **tool users** show what improved while keeping practical readings visible.
think: Our **higher covering wage**, existing flat and fourteen-month reserve make current living feel secure.
Unknown **later income figures** need checking without turning the next household bill into a crisis.
do: Keep **current paid repairs**, normal electrical tests and existing occasional checked AI explanations now and through the next year.
Ask our **grown daughter** for letter-sorting time only if willing and available, counting none of her money as ours.
feel: **Calm and organised**, glad to sort actual papers without pretending a tidy folder establishes affordable retirement.
S0.quote: A tidy folder would please me without proving when I could retire.
fieldNote: His **present security** has wage, housing and reserve support, without any pension payment or future job invented.
His **family request** concerns voluntary time, while existing occasional AI use creates neither new learning nor an automated household plan.

steps.text: Keep current paid repairs, normal tests and existing occasional checked AI explanations
Ask our grown daughter for willing available letter-sorting time, counting no money from her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say my physical work and Mina's translation work don't have the same exposure. I'd ask for practical teaching that somebody had actually tried before we paid for a place. I'd still judge a useful tool by what it helped somebody do correctly, not how confident the demonstration sounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mina could lose paid leaflet orders as writing and checking get cheaper, and I don't know how much her clients would retain. My practical repair work looks steadier, though faster planning could alter paid visits too. The reserve and my essential-covering wage give us control without making a reduction in household income irrelevant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in the training centre's test-meter record class only after confirming a place and employer payment of every fee and travel cost. I'd attend only inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages and hours maintained, learning to read the instrument's reports without gaining another licence. During the first year I'd keep current paid repairs and the existing occasional checked AI explanations, while comparing actual household income with essentials. I wouldn't count a class as Mina's replacement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost household earnings, and interested in a practical class after other people had shown its use. I'd be comfortable saying the firm needed to agree the paid arrangement first. Being able to pay today's bills doesn't make my partner's paid work unimportant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm paid the fee but cut the paid week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't enrol under this plan. I'd need the normal weekly wages and hours protected as well as the fees and travel covered. I'd keep the existing checked procedures while asking what actual funded teaching was available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that class protect you from later machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would help me read the records on work I actually do. I'd still be an experienced ordinary electrician, not a specialist with a protected title. I can choose useful teaching without advertising it as a lifetime guarantee.

fieldNote: His **conditional enrolment** requires a real place, complete employer funding and protected paid time, wages and hours.

steps.text: Enrol in test-meter record training only with confirmed place and employer paying all fees and travel
Enrol only with paid class time maintaining normal weekly wages and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I'd be 60 at thinking AGI and 63 when capable robots followed around 2031. Mina's leaflet income faces the first date more directly than my fitting work. I'd want actual paid terms, not reassurance that our age or flat answered the whole question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Mina's translation income to disappear around 2028, a large household loss even though my wage covers ordinary essentials now. Later robots could also cut my repair hours. I'd wake at night thinking about rebuilding dependable income, despite the flat and fourteen months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for posted licensed service jobs within my actual ability now, and in 2029 if income was still needed. I'd leave only for a signed offer with written weekly pay and guaranteed paid hours producing at least my current take-home after travel. I'd request available free evening community advice on actual income eligibility, amounts, dates and costs. I'd count no pension entitlement, unoffered family payment or job income before the actual terms existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected large household loss, with practical options rather than a feeling of having nowhere to turn. I'd still sleep badly over the gap. Owning our flat doesn't tell me who replaces my partner's translation fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apply if your current wage covers ordinary essentials?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I would want to test actual opportunities for dependable hours before any reduction in my own work. I'd require the written weekly income after travel to be at least what I currently take home. I wouldn't move for a friendly interview or a higher hourly rate without enough paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the advice suggested stopping work was affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd verify the actual income amounts, start dates, conditions and costs with Mina before agreeing an exit. An adviser offering to read the papers isn't an approved payment. Any work I counted in 2029 would need an actual offer within my ability then.

fieldNote: His **alarm** follows expected major partner-income loss and disturbed sleep, without denying the current wage and strong resources.
His **applications** require actual suitable work and guaranteed affordable terms, with no vacancy, future capacity or hiring assumed.

steps.text: Apply now and in 2029 if income needed for posted licensed service jobs within actual ability
Leave only for signed offers guaranteeing weekly pay and paid hours maintaining current take-home after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd be 63 at thinking AGI and 66 around the capable robot date. I'd use the time to test whether somebody would pay for a small practical demonstration, not call a new title an escape. Mina's translation still faces the earlier thinking change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of Mina's fees around 2031, and I don't know what dependable income would replace them. The extra time gives us choices but doesn't stop me doing sums when I should be asleep. A second small earning idea might be useful without replacing a whole working income or surviving robots forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd apply only for advertised Saturday demonstration shifts accepting my existing credentials and duties within my actual ability. I'd take at most one Saturday monthly only with employer permission, centre insurance, written fees covering travel, Mina agreeing the time and every normal paid shift retained. In 2032 I'd request available free evening advice to check actual resources, costs and capacity before any exit, requiring affordability and Mina's agreement. I'd count only actual paid offers within my ability, not a promised teaching career or a pension no one had confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the expected household loss, and still interested in trying one concrete earning option. I'd be careful not to make the demonstration sound more important because I wanted it to work. A Saturday fee could be useful without becoming my partner's missing year's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an ordinary electrician's licence qualify you for every demonstration post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd read the actual advertised requirements before applying. I'd offer only ordinary work I could explain and perform safely, not specialist instruction or independent authority I didn't hold. A training centre's name doesn't change the qualifications I actually have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you turn down a Saturday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Missing permission or insurance, fees that didn't cover travel, lost normal paid work or Mina not agreeing the time would stop it. I'd need the actual written fee before relying on an earning. I wouldn't assume any demonstration job or the physical ability to do it still existed in 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time for small checked decisions without choosing the last day of work now. I'd be 68 at thinking AGI and around 71 at the capable robot date. I'd still ask about actual income rather than assume our flat made every later cost disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical wage looks secure near term, but Mina could lose some paid orders as translation tools improve before full AGI. I don't know how much would go over the next few years, so the household income risk would still make me anxious. Our reserves and paid home give choices without proving later income, an offered job or physical ability at 69.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an extra 100 monthly cash deposit from new wages only after essentials and Mina's agreement, leaving the existing fourteen-month reserve untouched and stopping if surplus or consent disappeared. I'd keep current paid repairs and existing occasional checked AI explanations, counting no teaching income before an actual paid shift. I'd request available free evening advice now on actual income eligibility, amounts, dates and costs. In 2037 we'd check confirmed resources, actual costs, ability and genuine paid offers before any exit, requiring affordability and Mina's agreement rather than assume a pension or our children's money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost household income, though less alarmed by the distant date itself. I'd still enjoy doing the ordinary job and visiting the grown children. I wouldn't turn every family lunch into a discussion of what the family might pay us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the deposit had to stop after one month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it would stop instead of coming back out of the existing reserve. The deposit is extra only if actual wages leave the money after essentials and Mina still agrees. A regular transfer isn't a wage that the household owes to its own savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on doing repairs until robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd count only an actual offer within my ability then and only verified income elsewhere. Wanting the flat to remain comfortable doesn't create a paid job for my older body. We'd need actual resources and costs before agreeing when stopping was affordable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect most of Mina's translation income to go before we've checked a replacement, with capable robots reaching my physical work later around 2031. Actual paid terms, practical teaching without lost wages and understandable household income figures would help. I'd like an answer that tells us what is confirmed before it tells us to feel reassured.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the person with the tool is the person whose income is most exposed. I can use a proven AI explanation now and then while Mina's actual paid task faces the earlier change. Our household has two different working days inside one budget.

headlineQuote: Our household has two different working days inside one budget.
portrait: Tomas, **58**, is an experienced average mid-level electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary wiring and repairs.
He has **higher pay**, fourteen months saved, plenty of nearby firms and an owned flat, with translator partner Mina and grown children.
He uses **proven AI occasionally**, while practical classes require a real funded place and protected paid time, weekly wages and hours.
His **bounded demonstrations and deposits** require actual permissions, fees or wage surplus, while later exits depend on confirmed resources and Mina's agreement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** means expected loss of most of Mina’s translation income before a confirmed replacement, with repair robots following around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual paid terms**, practical teaching without lost wages and understandable household income figures would make confirmed resources visible before reassurance.
